newsitem.title: FRANCE: France welcomes U.S. plan for global landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: France welcomes U.S. plan for global landmine ban.

text.p: France on Saturday welcomed an announcement by the United States that it would seek a global ban on landmines at the Conference on Disarmament starting on Monday in Geneva.
"France is delighted with this decision," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"The campaign led by France, along with other nations including notably its European partners, for a universal and verifiable ban on anti-personnel landmines has been given a major boost with the American decision to accept negotiations on this subject at the Conference on Disarmament," the ministry said.
France announced its support for a total international ban on anti-personnel mines in May 1996, according to the statement.
France has also stopped producing and exporting landmines, the statement said, congratulating Washington for having decided unilaterally to take similar steps.
Officials announced in October that France would only use anti-personnel mines "in case of absolute necessity", to protect French forces.

The U.S. decision to pursue a ban through the Geneva negotiations appeared to be a blow to Canada's efforts to negotiate a ban through its "Ottawa process" of talks, which two key countries -- Russia and China -- have said they will not support.
U.S. officials said the decision reflected the conclusion that Geneva would be a more effective forum, not least because Russia and China would attend the talks.
The ban would apply only to anti-personnel landmines, which are designed to injure people, rather than anti-armour mines, which are made to destroy heavy vehicles like tanks.

Russia and China are seen as the primary global suppliers of landmines, more than 100 million of which lie buried or hidden in 64 countries around the world. Some 25,000 people a year are killed or maimed by mines left when wars end.
